title: An Interesting Similarity Between Ridley Scott's Napoleon and Stanley Kubrick's

commenti.body:
That's an interesting detail, and maybe a nod to Kubrick. I believe Scott mentioned in one of his interviews that he read Kubrick's Napoleon at some point and found it underwhelming. It tried to include absolutely everything from birth to death and Scott found it too much, or something like that.

Seems like Scott started out as a huge Kubrick fan, and probably still is, and Kubrick's influence is still obvious. Especially with The Duellists, which feels like it owes a large debt to Barry Lyndon. But recently Scott has been more critical of things like shooting too many takes, and said he thinks Stephen King's book was better than Kubrick's film of The Shining. Now that Scott has made Napoleon, which feels like coming full circle back to The Duellists and Kubrick, but Scott has now found his own voice. Maybe he includes some subtle nods to Kubrick, and the influence is still there, but Scott is also now very much his own person and in same ways extremely different.

Scott cites 2001 as the reason he decided to become a filmmaker. And of course, the Duelists was directly inspired by Barry Lyndon, and he got help from Kubrick when he made Blade Runner, where he got second unit helicopter footage from The Shining. He obviously admires him, but Scott's methods and to a certain extent his tastes are different. The same way Spielberg is also an enormous fan of Kubrick, and the way Kubrick was an enormous fan of Spielberg, despite the two having vastly different methods and styles.

That's a fascinating observation! Artists often borrow ideas from one another, intentionally or not, and the creative process often leads to these kinds of thematic correlations. The use of mirrors, in particular, might symbolize introspection, duality or a multitude of other philosophical concepts. Consider also the historical context: both filmmakers are depicting the same true events, so it's plausible that they might independently arrive at similar compositions.

This also brings up an interesting point on how filmmakers can carry the torch of unfinished projects from the past, intentionally or not. Reflecting on, how could other unmade masterpieces of past directors influence future cinema? Could this be considered an indirect form of homage to those unfinished works? I think these are interesting questions to delve into!
Given the context of the scene I would go with duplicity.
